details:
**The Name of the Rose**
Eco's first and most famous novel (1980), a medieval murder mystery set in 1327 at a Benedictine abbey in northern Italy. It is the near-universal giveaway for Eco.

**William of Baskerville and Adso of Melk**
The detective pair of The Name of the Rose. William is a Franciscan friar and former inquisitor whose name nods to Sherlock Holmes's "The Hound of the Baskervilles" and who was a student of William of Ockham. Adso, his young Benedictine novice, narrates the story as an old man. On arriving, William shows off his reasoning by deducing details about the abbot's runaway horse, Brunellus.

**Jorge of Burgos and Aristotle's Poetics**
Jorge is the blind old monk who is the villain of The Name of the Rose. He believes laughter is dangerous and sinful, so he hides the last surviving copy of the lost second book of Aristotle's Poetics, the one on comedy, and poisons its pages so that anyone who reads it dies. When cornered, he eats the poisoned pages.

**The finis Africae and the library fire**
The finis Africae is the secret sealed room of the abbey's labyrinthine library in the Aedificium, entered through a hidden passage behind a mirror. Jorge hides the Poetics there, and the novel ends with a fire that burns down the library and the abbey.

**Venantius, Berengar, Severinus, and Malachi**
Victims in The Name of the Rose's chain of murders. The translator Venantius is found head-down in a vat of pig's blood, where the assistant librarian Berengar had hidden his body; Berengar is later found drowned in the baths. The herbalist Severinus has his head smashed with an armillary sphere by the librarian Malachi, whom Jorge had made jealous. Malachi then dies from the poisoned book himself.

**Bernard Gui**
The real-life Dominican inquisitor who appears in The Name of the Rose. He arrives at the abbey, arrests a peasant girl as a witch along with the cellarer Remigio and the hunchback Salvatore, and has them condemned.

**Foucault's Pendulum**
Eco's 1988 novel about three Milan publishing editors who make up an occult conspiracy theory, called "the Plan," about the Knights Templar as a joke. Occultists come to believe it, and the joke turns deadly. It is famously dense, and Anthony Burgess joked that it needed an index.

**Casaubon, Belbo, and Diotallevi**
The three editors at Garamond Publishing (linked to the vanity press Manuzio) who create the Plan in Foucault's Pendulum. Casaubon narrates. At the start he is hiding at night in Paris's Musée des Arts et Métiers, and at the end he reads Belbo's files and reflects on his death. Diotallevi, a student of the Kabbalah, dies of cancer, which he sees as punishment for mocking sacred texts.

**Abulafia and the "telluric currents"**
Abulafia is Belbo's computer, named after a medieval Kabbalist, whose password is "no." The editors use it to randomly combine and rearrange facts into the Plan. They got the idea from Colonel Ardenti, who brought them a manuscript claiming the Templars had a secret plan to control the "telluric currents" of the earth, and who then disappeared.

**Agliè, the Tres, and the pendulum**
Count Agliè is a mysterious occultist in Foucault's Pendulum who hints that he is the immortal Count of Saint-Germain. He leads the believers who take the Plan seriously and become convinced that they are the "Tres," a fictional society the editors invented. At a ritual in the Musée des Arts et Métiers, Belbo's lover Lorenza is stabbed and Belbo is hanged from Foucault's pendulum.

**Baudolino**
Eco's 2000 novel about a gifted liar and polyglot peasant boy who is adopted by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. During the sack of Constantinople in the Fourth Crusade (1204), he saves the historian Niketas Choniates and tells him his life story, including how he solved Barbarossa's death in a locked room. His friends include the Archpoet and Kyot.

**Prester John, the Gavagai, and Alessandria**
The main quest in Baudolino is a journey to find the legendary Christian kingdom of Prester John. On the way, the travelers meet monsters such as Gavagai, a one-legged skiapod, and reach a land ruled by the leper Deacon John. Earlier, Baudolino's father saves the besieged city of Alessandria by feeding a cow huge amounts of grain to trick the besiegers into thinking the city has plenty of food.

**The Prague Cemetery**
Eco's 2010 novel about Captain Simone Simonini, an antisemitic forger who produces documents that become the Protocols of the Elders of Zion. He discovers that the Abbé Dalla Piccola is his own alter ego, and he recalls spying on Giuseppe Garibaldi. The novel also touches on the Dreyfus Affair, and Eco said that every character except Simonini was historical.

**The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana and The Island of the Day Before**
In The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana (2004), the rare-book dealer Yambo has a stroke that wipes out his personal memories but leaves him remembering everything he has read. In The Island of the Day Before (1994), the 17th-century nobleman Roberto della Griva is shipwrecked onto the abandoned Dutch ship Daphne and imagines an evil twin brother named Ferrante.

**Semiotics and nonfiction essays**
Eco was a scholar of semiotics (the study of signs) who wrote his dissertation on the aesthetics of Thomas Aquinas. His essays include Travels in Hyperreality, which describes Disneyland's audio-animatronics as more real than reality; How to Travel with a Salmon, in which he empties a hotel minibar to store a smoked salmon; On Ugliness; and The Infinity of Lists.
